name: PT Nusantara Sawit Sejahtera Tbk

frontmatter.title: Nusantara Sawit Sejahtera - young palms, crowded price
frontmatter.summary: A small, high-yield Central Kalimantan palm producer whose equity price discounts a CPO price well above our deck and an enterprise value per planted hectare above the only cited transaction comparable. The estate is genuinely good and the third mill is funded; the risk is what the market already pays for it, plus a qualified audit opinion and a concentrated register.
thesis: NSSS runs a young planted estate at a high FFB yield and oil extraction rate, among the better young plantings in the listed set, and sells all of its CPO and kernel domestically.
The 2026 cost step is in the filing, not in our caution - labour and purchased FFB lifted unit cash cost well above the audited FY2025 level, so FY2026E EBITDA is flat to down despite higher prices.
Our through-cycle DCF values the equity below the market price; the market price implies a CPO price well above the reviewed deck.

Governance is the discount, not a footnote - a qualified FY2025 opinion over the SK forest-area finding, a small free float and a handful of buyers taking most of sales; the IDX trading-concentration review is supervision, not a finding, and NSSS's 52% share was the lowest of the three names examined.

Growth is real but capped - the third mill adds capacity in the 2027-28 phase and a large landbank is unplanted, yet existing mills limit CPO output without further planting; we value the unplanted landbank at a sourced transaction discount, not at zero.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and the dividend declaration
Third CPO mill (second-phase capacity expansion) construction and capex commitment disclosure
IDX trading-concentration review outcome for the December-2025 to October-2026 window

blocks.text: We initiate NSSS at **SELL** with a target of **Rp336**, -33.1% from the last price of Rp510. The company is a Central Kalimantan palm-oil producer with 28,204.0 hectares planted, a young tree profile, two mills and a strategy of selling everything into the domestic market [S4]. The estate is not the problem. The price is. At Rp510 the equity is worth IDR12,138.8bn, and after net debt the enterprise value is roughly IDR663.4bn higher again on our forecast, which is an enterprise value per planted hectare well above the only transaction comparable this report cites [S7], and 12.9x times forward EBITDA [S0, S4, S7]. Our through-cycle discounted cash flow, which prices CPO off the reviewed agri deck rather than the spot print, values the equity at Rp386 per share [S0].

The variant view is not that the palms are bad — they are good. It is that the market is paying for a CPO price that the deck does not support and for a volume curve the current mills cannot deliver. The reverse DCF says the current price requires a CPO price of US$1,522/t against our FY2027E deck marker of 1,240.0 USD/t [S0], a factor of 1.2 on the base case. Two other things move the value. First, unit cash cost: the nine-month 2026 filing shows a cash cost per tonne of CPO far above the audited FY2025 level, a step driven by direct labour and purchased FFB that we carry forward rather than fade [S2, F7, F9]. Second, governance: the FY2025 opinion is qualified over the SK forest-area decision, IDX is reviewing trading concentration in the shares, the free float is 21.3%, and the shares have sat on IDX's special-monitoring board under full call auction since January 2026 [S3, S6, S8, S9, S0].

We are not bearish on the asset. In the bull case, where the deck price runs a fifth above base, volume runs above plan and the realised discount narrows back toward the audited FY2025 level, the shares are worth Rp499 — still below today's Rp510 [S0]. That is the core of the call: the market price is above even our bull case, so the distribution of outcomes is skewed against the buyer at this price, and the base case is the most likely path, not a cautious one. The largest single downside not in the base is quantified in the footnote to the FY2025 audit: applying PP45 in full would add about IDR368.0bn of G&A and IDR78.0bn of other operating expense, and we carry the booked provision only [S3, F28].

NSSS is an integrated palm-oil producer: it cultivates oil palm, harvests fresh fruit bunches (FFB), and mills them into crude palm oil (CPO) and palm kernel (PK) [S5]. The group is a holding company over five operating subsidiaries — Nusantara Sawit Persada (NSP), Borneo Sawit Perdana (BSP), Prasetya Mitra Muda (PMM), Bina Sarana Sawit Utama (BSSU) and Hamparan Mitra Abadi (HMA) — all located in Kotawaringin Timur, Gunung Mas and Kapuas in Central Kalimantan [S3]. The company was founded in 2008 and listed on IDX in March 2023 [S4]. It operates as a single segment, palm oil, and reports no other line of business [S2].

The asset base is 28,204.0 hectares planted across the nucleus estates, plus 16,501.0 hectares of unplanted landbank for expansion, for a total of about forty-four thousand hectares under HGU and permits [S4, S5]; the unplanted landbank is carried as a separate valuation item in the valuation section, not at zero and not as free volume [F22]. Processing is two CPO mills with combined capacity of 120.0 tonnes per hour of FFB, or seven hundred and twenty thousand tonnes a year, supported by direct piping to special terminals [S4]. The third mill at PMM is planned for the 2027-28 capacity-expansion phase at an estimated capex of Rp270.0bn, adding up to sixty tonnes per hour and expected to lift the oil extraction rate further [S4].

The revenue mix is simple and fully domestic: CPO and palm kernel, sold to three buyers who take the large majority of sales, of which the largest, PT Sinar Mas Agro Resources and Technology, is 52.0% [S3]. There is no export book, no refinery and no oleochemical downstream; the company's own presentation describes a revenue structure of entirely domestic sales, which insulates it from the one-door export policy but ties it to the Indonesian reference price [S4]. In FY2025 CPO sales were 122.3 kt at Rp13,930 per kg (USD 846.9/t at the FY2025 exchange rate) and PK sales 26.7 kt at Rp11,598.0 per kg, together producing revenue of IDR2,013.8bn [F5]. CPO is close to nine tenths of revenue and essentially all of the gross profit; kernel is a by-product [S5].

The controlling structure is concentrated. PT Samuel Tumbuh Bersama held about two fifths of the shares at the end of 2025 alongside related Samuel entities and the president director's personal holding, and the IDX free float is 21.3% of the register, while the public register (non-controlling shareholders, including sub-threshold board holdings) is 31.8% [S5, S0]. The board is led by Teguh Patriawan, who is also a substantial shareholder [S5]. This is a family- and sponsor-controlled small cap, not an institutionally held estate.

Strategy, as the company describes it, is to mature the existing plantings, lift mill utilisation toward higher throughput, add the third mill, and keep amortising the BRI and BMRI facilities that built the estates [S4, S3]. There is no announced acquisition programme and no downstream integration plan.

Indonesia is the world's largest palm-oil producer. The company's own annual report puts national CPO production, exports of palm oil and derivatives and domestic demand, the last lifted by the biodiesel mandate that began in January 2025 [S5]. The higher blend mandate started in mid-2026, and the company expects it to raise domestic absorption and tighten export supply [S4]. That is the structural demand story behind the deck's price path: our reviewed agri deck carries CPO at 1,007.0 USD/t for FY2025A, 1,135.0 USD/t for FY2026E, 1,240.0 USD/t for FY2027E and a long-run marker of 1,150.0 USD/t escalating with inflation [S0]. The World Bank re-based its palm-oil series from January 2026, which is why the 2026 monthly tape and the pre-2026 annual averages are not perfectly homogeneous [S0].

The regulation that matters most for this name is not the export levy — NSSS sells domestically and carries no royalty or levy line in cost of sales [S3, S4]. It is the forestry amnesty. On 6 February 2025 the Minister of Environment and Forestry issued Decision Letter SK, identifying palm companies, including two NSSS subsidiaries, as operating inside forest areas without the required forestry permits; PP 45 of 2025 set the enforcement mechanism and the fine formula [S3]. The group booked a Rp56.7bn provision for administrative fines and a Rp51.7bn fixed-asset impairment at 31 December 2025 [S2, F28, F29], and the FY2025 audit opinion is qualified on that uncertainty [S3]. This is the single largest regulatory overhang on the equity, and it is unresolved as of this report.

Competitive position is a niche one. NSSS is a small producer: at about 122.3 kt of CPO in FY2025 it is a fraction of the size of the listed peers in our plantation coverage, which run several hundred thousand tonnes each [S5, S0]. Its edge is agronomic rather than scale: a first-half nucleus FFB yield of 9.7 t/ha — about nineteen to twenty tonnes per hectare on an annual basis, since FY2025's 541.1 kt of harvested FFB over 28,204.0 ha implies an annual yield of about nineteen to twenty tonnes per hectare [F35, F21] — and an OER of 22.5%, with the majority of plantings still approaching optimal maturity, which the company argues delivers lower transport, processing and oil-loss costs than peers [S4]. The tree profile is young, so the yield curve still rises without new land; that is a genuine advantage over estates with ageing palms.

The moat, though, is thin in the five-forces sense. CPO is a commodity with no pricing power: the company is a price taker against the Indonesian reference price, and its three domestic buyers take the large majority of volume, which gives the buyers the bargaining power [S3]. Barriers to entry are land, permits and capex, not technology. Substitutes are other vegetable oils — the deck carries soyoil at 1,556.7 USD/t and soymeal at 411.0 USD/t for FY2026E — and the substitution channel runs through price [S0]. Supplier power is moderate: fertiliser and labour are the swing costs, and the 2026 cost step shows how quickly they move [S2].

On cost we make one sourced comparison rather than place NSSS on a cost curve we have not built. Its nine-month cash cost per tonne of CPO equals about 508.3 USD/t at the forecast exchange rate [S0, S2], which is competitive for an Indonesian estate of this size but not the low-cost end of the set. That position survives a trough but does not compound through it. Reserve life is not the right frame for palms; the equivalent discipline is planted area and tree age, and here the company has 28,204.0 hectares of young planted estate and 16,501.0 hectares of landbank, which gives it a long production life rather than a depleting one [S4].

The macro frame the desk carries is cautious: the balance-of-payments pressure regime is CAUTIOUS and the rupiah is weak, with the deck at Rp17,570 per dollar for FY2026E against a spot of Rp18,080 [S0]. A weak rupiah helps a domestic-price seller only if the domestic reference price follows the dollar print; the 2026 evidence is that it lagged, which is exactly why our realisation ratio sits below the audited FY2025 level [S0, S2].

Palm oil is the highest-yielding major oilseed per hectare, and Indonesia and Malaysia together
supply most of the world's traded volume. Estate economics are driven by three things: the age profile
of the palms, the oil extraction rate at the mill, and the gap between the fruit price paid and the
crude palm oil sold. Young estates produce rising volumes for a decade before plateauing, which is why
planted area and planting vintage matter more than a single year's output. Plantation companies
typically trade on a blend of discounted cash flow and enterprise value per planted hectare, because
accounting earnings swing violently with the commodity price while the asset base does not.

Revenue grew from IDR1,489.9bn in FY2024 to IDR2,013.8bn in FY2025, a 35.2% increase driven by both volume and price: CPO sales rose to 122.3 kt and the realised CPO price to Rp13,930 per kg (USD 846.9/t at the FY2025 average exchange rate), while kernel sales rose to 26.7 kt and the kernel price to Rp11,598.0 per kg [S5, F1, F3, F14, F15]. Gross profit rose from IDR584.8bn to IDR1,094.2bn, a 54.3% margin, and net profit rose to IDR647.8bn [F11]. That FY2025 net profit already carries the SK charges — the Rp56.7bn fine provision and the Rp51.7bn asset impairment — but the EBITDA we model is on the pack's adjusted basis, not the audited operating result: IDR1,106.4bn is the pack's EBIT of IDR950.3bn plus the LK depreciation charge of IDR156.1bn, and that EBIT sits above audited income from operations of IDR894.4bn because the pack treats the other operating expenses tied to Decree No. 36 as non-recurring [S2, S0, S3, F28, F29, F44]. Those are the IDR57.7bn of other operating expenses the filing shows, and we keep the adjusted basis deliberately: the base year is the operating run-rate before the charge, and the charge itself is carried only where the booking is known [S3, F45].

The 2026 picture is different, and it is the reason our numbers sit below the run-rate that the first half suggested. Nine-month revenue rose to IDR1,742.6bn, but cost of goods sold rose by about half on a year earlier, with FY2025 depreciation charged to operations of IDR156.1bn on sales of IDR2,013.8bn [S2, F33, F9]. Strip out depreciation and the cash cost for the nine months is still close to nine hundred billion rupiah. Two lines explain the step. Raw materials used roughly quadrupled, because the mills are buying external FFB to fill capacity, and direct labour and supporting materials rose by about half [S2]. On the CPO sold in the nine months that leaves a unit cash cost well above the audited FY2025 level, and we carry it in the forecast [S2, F7, F9]. Nine-month net profit fell to IDR501.3bn [S2].

We carry that unit cost, escalated with inflation, rather than the FY2025 level. That is the honest reading of the last actual, and it is why FY2026E EBITDA of IDR995.9bn is slightly below FY2025's rather than above it [S0]. Revenue for FY2026E is IDR2,270.3bn — CPO volume of 130.0 kt at a realised price of 862.6 USD/t equivalent, plus kernel revenue of IDR300.0bn. The realised price carries a 76.0% realisation against a benchmark of 1,135.0 USD/t [S0]. Cash cost is IDR1,160.9bn, depreciation IDR161.2bn, and operating expenses IDR113.5bn, leaving an EBITDA margin of 43.9% [S0].

The forecast path then improves with the deck. CPO rises to 1,240.0 USD/t in FY2027E before easing to 1,210.0 USD/t and 1,180.0 USD/t, volume grows from 130.0 kt to 147.0 kt as the young plantings mature and the third mill lifts throughput, and costs escalate at inflation [S0, S4]. FY2027E EBITDA is IDR1,252.4bn and EPS Rp32 [S0]. We do not assume the oil extraction rate rises to the target level before the new mill is commissioned, and we do not assume any recovery in the realised-price ratio — the deck alone moves the price.

Cash flow is the strong part of the story. Operating cash flow was IDR868.8bn in FY2025 and stayed strong in the nine months of 2026 even after a short-term investment placement and the dividend [S3, S2, F31]. Capex was IDR101.3bn of fixed-asset additions in FY2025, plus plasma receivables and nursery/land-clearing spending, which we carry together at about the FY2025 unit rate in the forecast [S3, S2]. The balance sheet is leveraged but manageable: bank debt was above one and a half trillion rupiah at 30 September 2026 against cash of Rp678.2bn and the short-term investment of Rp227.0bn. We restart the debt schedule from that 30 September 2026 balance and book the observed nine-month repayment, so FY2026E debt is IDR1,575.3bn against IDR1,765.5bn at end-2025 and net debt is IDR663.4bn on our year-end forecast, 0.7 times EBITDA [S2]. Interest cover is comfortable at these prices and thin in the bear case, which is the classic plantation balance-sheet shape.

Capital allocation is straightforward: amortise the BRI/BMRI facilities, fund the third mill from cash flow, and pay a modest dividend. The group paid IDR119.0bn in the first nine months of 2026 — the FY2025 dividend of Rp5 per share [S3, F31]. We model a 20.0% payout, which yields about 0.9% at the current price [S0]. There is no buyback and no rights issue in the record.

Earnings quality is where the file needs care. The accruals picture is clean on the cash test — net profit of IDR647.8bn against operating cash flow of IDR868.8bn, so earnings are backed by cash — but four items deserve flags. First, working capital: receivables plus inventories less payables were about a tenth of revenue at the end of FY2025, and inventories at 30 September 2026 are large against a quarter of cost of sales [S3, S2]. Second, the biological-asset fair-value line: a gain in the nine months of 2026 and a similar gain a year earlier run through profit, and we exclude it from the base as a mark rather than cash [S2]. Third, the SK provision and impairment are judgemental estimates of an unresolved administrative process, and a revision either way is possible [S2, S3]. The FY2025 audit note quantifies the gap: had PP45 been applied in full, G&A would be IDR368.0bn higher and other operating expenses IDR78.0bn higher — with accrued expenses, a balance-sheet line, also IDR368.0bn higher — fixed assets IDR78.0bn lower and the deferred tax liability and tax expense IDR114.0bn lower, against the Rp56.7bn provision and Rp51.7bn impairment actually booked [S3, F36, F46, F37, F38]. Fourth, the nine months carried Rp40.0bn of other operating income on the "Lainnya" line; we treat it as non-recurring and exclude it from the base, which is why the 9M26 net profit is not directly comparable with our FY2026E [S2, F47]. That is a pre-tax hit larger than the booked provision and impairment combined — a real bear-case tail, not a rounding item; the base carries only the booked provision. None of these is a manipulation-class flag; together they argue for valuing the cash flow, not the earnings headline.

We value NSSS on a through-cycle discounted cash flow, cross-checked against enterprise value to EBITDA and price to book, with weights of 60.0%, 25.0% and 15.0% [S0]. The method set fits a commodity producer: earnings swing with the CPO price while the asset base — planted hectares, mills, tree age — is stable, so a life-of-asset cash flow at a sourced through-cycle price is the right primary, and asset and earnings multiples are secondary sanity checks. Per the house commodity card, the frame carries the complex and the macro tilt alongside the name's own NAV: the deck, not the spot print, sets the marker, and the spot deviation is cycle position rather than value [S0].

Our through-cycle CPO price is the reviewed agri deck: the World Bank Pink Sheet history for FY2023A to FY2025A and the forward strip and reference-price evidence behind FY2026E to FY2029E, with a long-run marker of 1,150.0 USD/t escalating with inflation [S0]. That is a sourced series, not a felt number. The realisation applied to it is 76.0%, calibrated on the 2026 actuals rather than on the FY2025 audited ratio, because the World Bank re-based the palm series in January 2026 and the domestic price NSSS realises lagged the international print [S0, S2].

The cost of capital is built from the desk's market parameters. The Indonesian risk-free rate is 7.4%, but the house convention nets off the 1.6% sovereign default spread in the cost of equity, so the rf actually entering the build is the net figure; add the equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%, apply the unlevered beta of 0.80 relevered to 0.88, and the cost of equity is 11.7% — the arithmetic is 7.4% less 1.6% plus 0.88 times the sum of the 4.2% equity risk premium and the 2.5% country risk premium. The debt cost in the WACC is 9.4% pre-tax, which is the market build of the risk-free rate plus the corporate debt spread; that is a different number from the 8.5% marginal rate used in the P&L for the existing BRI/BMRI facilities, because the valuation prices new debt at market rather than the historical coupon. With a 11.5% debt weight the WACC is 11.2% [S0]. A one-percentage-point higher WACC would cut the DCF value by roughly a tenth and a half-point change in terminal growth by a similar order: the terminal value is 47.9% of enterprise value, so the discount rate and the terminal growth assumption, not the near-term cash flows, are the DCF's main sensitivity [S0].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR9,370.9bn, or Rp386 per share, with the terminal value at 47.9% of the total [S0]. After net debt and the short-term investment, and including the separately sourced landbank bridge set out below, the equity is worth Rp386. Spread across 28,204 planted hectares, that enterprise value is well above the IDR14,800.0bn paid for 128,000 ha in the only transaction evidence this report cites; the DCF's per-hectare value is therefore a clear premium to that comparable, not a market-consistent check [S7, F21, F41, F42]. We disclose the premium rather than explain it away: the DCF values a going concern with a funded third mill and a young tree profile whose volumes still rise, while the comparable is a control sale of a mature estate, so the cash-flow method — not the per-hectare read — is what carries the target. The sensitivity table shows the two drivers that matter: a hundred dollars a tonne on the CPO price moves the value by roughly a seventh, and a ten percent move in unit cash cost moves it by about three quarters as much in the opposite direction [S0]. The grid reports the blended value before the final twelve-month roll-forward, so its centre sits a few percent below the stated target.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative — but in the direction the red team established, not the one an earlier draft claimed. The peer-median EV/EBITDA approach gives Rp252 at 5.6 times trailing EBITDA, -34.7% versus the DCF [S0]: the house plantation peer set is cheap, and NSSS's own forward 12.9x multiple is far above it. The book-value cross-check gives Rp124 at 1.3 times, -67.8% versus the DCF, and that divergence needs explaining rather than hiding: a peer-median P/BV is the wrong anchor for a young estate earning a mid-twenties return on equity, where a justified P/BV on the name's own return, cost of equity and growth would be several times book. The peer median reflects the distressed end of the Indonesian plantation set, not NSSS's asset quality; it is why this cross-check carries only a 15.0% weight. Both multiples are therefore labelled honestly as peer medians. We do NOT blend NSSS's own post-IPO means into either: the stock listed in March 2023, there is no five-year history, and the handful of observations are drawn from the same Rp366 to Rp2,180 price spike the report itself says is not a valuation signal [S0]. The DCF keeps the majority weight because it is the only method that prices the deck rather than the peer set or the stock's own tape.

The 16,501.0 hectares of unplanted landbank are a separate bridge item — not zero, and not free volume. There is no unplanted-land transaction in our record; the nearest registered comp is POSCO International's November-2025 acquisition of control of Sampoerna Agro, which added 128,000 ha of oil-palm plantations for about IDR14,800.0bn [S7]. That price is for a planted, operating estate with mills and going-concern value attached, so we carry NSSS's unplanted land at a quarter of its implied per-hectare value: deliberately conservative, inside the range the red team framed, and a modest addition to the DCF rather than a value on which the rating turns [S7, F41, F42, F22]. Because the base credits no volume from planting beyond the annual new-planting programme, the associated land-clearing capex is removed from capex_unit, so the landbank is neither charged against an unvalued asset nor double-counted.

No separate liquidity haircut is applied to the target: three-month ADTV is IDR4.3bn a day, above the fund's stated ADTV floor at which the house begins to haircut, so the rule returns 0.0% [S0]. That 0.0% needs the mechanism beside it, because NSSS has traded on IDX's special-monitoring board (papan pemantauan khusus) under the full-call-auction mechanism since 20 January 2026 and no longer trades in the regular market [S8]; it is absent from the 29 September 2026 list of names removed from the board [S9]. The ADTV above is therefore auction turnover, not continuous-session turnover, and the discount rule — which is calibrated on regular-market ADTV — cannot be read as evidence of tradability. We keep the 0.0% because the house rule is a price-impact haircut and the auction price is the price, but the investability conclusion does not rest on it: the fund's universe rule admits main-board names only, and NSSS fails that test on the disclosed status regardless of turnover [S8, S9]. The risk is carried in the bear case and in the multiple discount, not in a second haircut.

What the price implies is the cleanest statement of the gap. At Rp510 the reverse DCF requires a CPO price of US$1,522/t, a factor of 1.2 on our base case, against a deck marker of 1,240.0 USD/t for FY2027E and a spot print of 1,180.0 USD/t [S0]. Alternatively, the forward EV/EBITDA of 12.9x and price-to-book of 5.1x are at or above the peer median on a lower-quality register. The equity is priced for the El Nino price spike and a clean regulatory outcome at the same time.

The dividend anchor is weak here, unlike the coal names: a 0.9% forward yield at a 20.0% payout does not support the price on its own, and the market is clearly not valuing NSSS on dividend capacity [S0]. The anchor the market is using is the CPO price and the growth option in the landbank. Our anchor is the NAV.

Through-cycle valuation for a plantation rests on the long-run incentive price for vegetable oil,
which is set by the cost of the marginal hectare of new supply, mostly in Indonesia and Malaysia, and
by the demand pull of biodiesel mandates. Because a palm estate lives for about twenty-five years,
the value is dominated by the terminal value and by the assumption that prices and costs escalate
together. The common error is to capitalise a spot or peak-year margin, which is why a cycle-aware
DCF will usually sit below a market price set during a price spike.
The risks, in order of what would hurt most:

**Regulatory — SK forest area (likelihood: high that it persists, impact: medium).** Two subsidiaries were identified as operating in forest areas without forestry permits, a Rp56.7bn fine provision and a Rp51.7bn impairment are booked, and the audit opinion is qualified [S2, S3, F28, F29]. A worse outcome could remove planted area from the estate base; a better one could release the provision. The FY2025 audit note puts a number on the downside: full PP45 application would raise G&A by IDR368.0bn and other operating expenses by IDR78.0bn, cut fixed assets by IDR78.0bn and cut the deferred tax liability and tax expense by IDR114.0bn, against the IDR56.7bn provision and IDR51.7bn impairment actually booked [S3, F36, F46, F37, F38]. Net of the IDR114.0bn tax effect that is a hit larger than the booked provision and impairment combined — a bear-case item, and the reason the base's clean opex ratio is explicitly an assumption about settlement, not a view that PP45 is harmless. Either way the overhang caps the multiple until it is resolved.

**Commodity price (likelihood: certain to move, impact: high).** Every hundred dollars a tonne on CPO is worth roughly a seventh of the equity value on the current sensitivity grid [S0]. The base case already uses a realised price well below the benchmark, so the downside is a deck undershoot rather than a realisation miss.

**Cost inflation (likelihood: medium-high, impact: medium-high).** The 2026 step in labour and purchased FFB is the single biggest change in the model [S2]. If it persists at the nine-month level, FY2027E margins are thinner than the deck implies; if it reverses, our base is conservative. We have taken the filing at face value rather than assume a reversal.

**Governance and liquidity (likelihood: high that it persists, impact: high).** NSSS has been on IDX's special-monitoring board (papan pemantauan khusus) under the full-call-auction mechanism since 20 January 2026 — the exchange's general rule puts a name on that board under its trading-activity criterion, which includes a suspension lasting beyond a single trading day, though the archived report does not state NSSS's own trigger [S8] — and it does not appear in the 29 September 2026 list of names removed from the board or the FCA [S8, S9]. The practical consequence is severe and is not a footnote: there is no continuous market, entry and exit happen only in auction sessions, and the fund's universe rule admits main-board names only, so NSSS is outside the BUY universe whatever its valuation [S8, S9]. IDX is separately reviewing trading concentration in NSSS over December 2025 to October 2026, during which a group of nineteen investors through fifteen brokers accounted for about half of transactions [S6]. BEI stressed that the review is a supervision step, not a finding of wrongdoing, and NSSS's concentration was the LOWEST of the three names examined (CASA and FUJI were higher), over the longest window and with the most participants [S6]. The discount here is the board status, the thin float of 21.3% and the controlled register, not the review [S5, S0]. A stock with this ownership, this tape and this trading mechanism can move far from value in both directions; that is a risk to being right, not a reason to be wrong.

**Operational (likelihood: medium, impact: medium).** El Nino is forecast to peak between late 2026 and early 2027 and could hit FFB yields; the company itself frames this as a price positive and a volume risk [S4]. Mill downtime, the third-mill construction and plasma-collection issues are the other operational levers.

**Balance sheet and currency (likelihood: low-medium, impact: medium).** Net debt of about IDR663.4bn and 0.7 times EBITDA is comfortable at base prices and uncomfortable in a trough [S0]. Debt is rupiah-denominated, so a weaker rupiah does not create a translation loss, but it raises the cost of refinancing if the deck's rate path is wrong [S0, S2].

**Related-party and concentration (likelihood: medium, impact: low-medium).** most of sales go to three buyers, the largest a majority [S3]. No related-party revenue concentration is disclosed in the audited segments, but the controlling shareholders' other vehicles are the natural counterparties to watch [S5].

The scenarios are mirrored around the same three drivers. In the bear case the CPO deck falls a fifth, volume runs five percent below plan and the realised ratio slips with the benchmark, giving a value of Rp156 at a 25.0% probability. In the bull case price runs a fifth above the deck, volume runs above plan as OER and maturing yields lift throughput, and the realisation recovers toward the audited FY2025 ratio, giving Rp499 at 25.0%. Base is Rp345 at 50.0% [S0]. The base probability is the highest, as it should be; the CPO and realisation shocks are mirrored, while the bull volume shock is one point stronger than the bear's, an asymmetry the audit judged immaterial because even the bull value sits below today's price. below today's price: the market is not merely discounting the base, it is pricing a better-than-bull outcome.

The signposts that would change our view are concrete. A sustained CPO print above 1,240.0 USD/t with the domestic realisation ratio recovering toward the audited FY2025 level would lift our value toward the bull case. A resolution of SK that removes the qualified opinion would compress the governance discount. Conversely, a cost run-rate that shows labour and purchased FFB normalising would make our base too conservative, and we would raise it. A confirmation that the third mill's capacity and OER uplift arrive on time would add volume beyond 2030 that we do not credit today.

Ownership is the first thing a reader should see. PT Samuel Tumbuh Bersama held about two fifths of the shares at the end of 2025, the president director held a further tenth in his own name, PT Nusantara Makmur Lestari held under a tenth and another Samuel entity held a similar stake; the IDX free float is 21.3%, while the public register (non-controlling holders) is 31.8% [S5, S0] — the two measures differ and the smaller one is the tradable float. There is no pledge disclosure in the audited accounts, and no rights issue or private placement in the record we reviewed [S3, S2]. The concentration is a structural fact rather than a scandal, but it explains both the tape and the discount.

The auditor is a member firm of Ernst & Young Global, and the FY2025 opinion is qualified — "wajar dengan pengecualian" — over the SK forest-area decision and the resulting uncertainty on asset carrying values and administrative sanctions [S3]. That is an optics-class flag, not a manipulation-class one: the issue is disclosed, quantified in part, and being processed with the authorities. But a qualified opinion is a qualified opinion, and it belongs in the price.

Related-party gravity is moderate. The group discloses plasma-plantation arrangements, receivables from plasma cooperatives at 30 September 2026, and a related-party cash and deposit relationship with Bank Panin entities [S2]. Plasma schemes are standard in the Indonesian industry and the receivables are a financing exposure rather than a related-party sale; we flag the collection risk, not a governance abuse. Sales are to third-party buyers, with SMAR at 52.0% of revenue [S3].

The trading-concentration review is the item a new investor should read carefully. IDX examined NSSS transactions over a window spanning late 2025 to late 2026 and found that nineteen investors through fifteen brokers accounted for about half of transactions, the widest window and the largest number of participants of the three stocks reviewed [S6]. The exchange stressed that the review is a supervision step, not a finding of wrongdoing [S6]. Still, a price that ran from a low of Rp366 to a high of Rp2,180 within a year on a thin float is not a price to trust as a valuation signal [S0].

The trading venue itself is the first governance fact for a new holder. Since 20 January 2026 NSSS has been listed on IDX's special-monitoring board (papan pemantauan khusus) and trades only through the full-call-auction mechanism; under the exchange's general rule a name enters that board on its trading-activity criterion, which includes a suspension lasting beyond a single trading day, and the shares no longer trade in the regular market [S8]. The public record we hold states that rule and the placement date, not NSSS's own criterion, so we do not attribute a specific trigger to it. NSSS is not among the names IDX removed from the special-monitoring board and FCA on 29 September 2026, so the status was still in force at the date of this report [S9]. For the house this is close to dispositive on investability: the universe rule is main-board only, so the name cannot be bought here regardless of value, and the 0.0% liquidity discount in the valuation applies to auction turnover rather than a continuous market [S8, S9]. We state the rating as a view on value, not as an entry recommendation.

The dividend record is short but real: the first dividend was paid in 2025 at Rp3 per share, and the FY2025 dividend of Rp5 per share was paid in 2026; the trailing twelve-month distribution is Rp8 per share at a modest payout [S3, F31, S0]. The board is small and family-led, with a president commissioner and a president director; there is no evidence of board independence problems beyond the ownership concentration [S5].

ESG exposure is dominated by the forest-area issue. The company holds ISPO certification for NSP and BSP and targets full ISPO for BSSU and then HMA, and publishes a sustainability report alongside the annual report [S4, S5]. ISPO certification does not settle the SK question — the company's own communications note that the estates are ISPO-certified yet still claimed to be within forest areas [S5]. Labour practices, smallholder plasma obligations and land-conflict risk are the industry's standard ESG channels, and NSSS carries them at a small-cap scale with limited disclosure [S5].

Indonesian plantation governance has a well-known pattern: a founder or sponsor group holds a
majority, the free float is small, and the market price can diverge from fundamental value for long
periods because few shares trade. The forestry amnesty of recent years was designed to regularise
estates that had operated for years inside designated forest land, in exchange for fines and, in some
cases, land release. For investors, the practical question is not whether the process is fair but
whether the provision booked is the final number.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027, the third-mill construction start and capex disclosure, the IDX review outcome, and any movement in the SK case [S3, S4, S6, S2]. The FY2026 results matter most because they will show whether the nine-month cost step was a run-rate or a spike: labour, raw materials used and factory overhead are the three lines to read [S2].
Between updates we monitor, in order:

items: **Monthly CPO reference price and the realised spread.** The deck's monthly Pink Sheet prints and the
Indonesian reference price are the input to everything; the realised ratio is the company-specific
**Quarterly FFB harvested, yield and OER.** Compare the half-year yield against 9.7

below 22.5% would signal the El Nino hitting the estate [S4, F35, F21].
**Unit cash cost.** The nine-month unit cash cost is the number to beat or confirm [S2].
**SK and PP 45.** Any ministerial decision, fine revision or land release [S2, S3].
**IDX and OJK notices.** Trading supervision, free-float compliance and any disclosure of
shareholding changes among the controlling group [S6, S5].
**Third-mill progress.** Capex spend against the Rp270.0bn estimate and the commissioning

bear.narrative: CPO falls back to the deck trough and the domestic discount widens: the re-based benchmark drops 20%, CPO sales run 5% below plan and the realised ratio slips to 0.69 (the 2026 discount persists) as the cost step runs to the PP45 quantification and El Nino hits FFB yields. At that price and a Rp8.9m/t cash cost the margin is thin and the third mill is deferred; the Rp368bn PP45 exposure would take another ~Rp11/share if it were booked.

bull.narrative: The El Nino lifts 2027 CPO prices and the deck runs 20% above base; the third mill's new technology lifts OER toward 23%, maturing palms lift volume 6% above plan, and the domestic discount narrows back toward the audited FY2025 ratio (0.841) as B50 absorbs supply, so the 2027 margin expansion holds through the cycle.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: CPO sales volume (kt)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E of 130 kt is built from the nine-month run-rate: 1H2026 CPO sales were 61.2 kt (+5.5% yoy, [F18]) on CPO production of 64.0 kt (+8.7%, OER 22.5%, [F17, F24]), and the Q3 statement implies roughly 99 kt of CPO sold in the nine months against harvested FFB of 401 kt [F20, F33]. Q4 is the normal peak quarter (Q4-2025 was 522bn of revenue, 26% of the year [S3]), giving about 130 kt for FY2026E, +6.3% on the audited 122.3 kt [F1]. The yield basis is ANNUAL: FY2025 harvested FFB was 541.1 kt over 28,204 planted ha [F35, F21], about 19.2 t/ha; the 9.7 t/ha in the 1H26 presentation [F23] is a half-year figure (two quarters of 5.2 and 4.5 t/ha), not an annual one. The mills ran at 78% utilisation in FY2025 and the company guides to ~80%, or 576 kt FFB on 720,000 t capacity, at 22.5% OER = 129.6 kt CPO [F25, F24, S4]; so FY2026E and FY2027E are held at the utilisation guidance (130 and 132 kt), not grown. From FY2028E the company's phase-02 (2027-28) third mill adds up to 60 t/hr "to support maturing estate yield curves" and new mill technology lifts OER "up to 23% from current 22%" [S4, F32]; the ~1,500 ha/yr new plantings [S4] and maturing palms then carry volume to 138 kt in FY2028E and 147 kt by FY2030E, with the long-run capped at 150 kt, below the post-third-mill 1,080,000 t FFB capacity at 80% utilisation. Purchased FFB is held near the 9M26 run-rate (~60 kt annualised), not at the 132 kt implied only by a constant-harvest assumption [S2]. The 16,501 ha unplanted landbank beyond the ~1,500 ha/yr programme is a long-run option and is not in this line [F22].

assumptions.label: Realised CPO price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated on the last actual, not on a spike year. The audited FY2025 realised price of Rp13,930/kg [F3] was 0.841 of the FY2025 Pink Sheet average of USD 1,007/t at Rp16,448/USD [S0]. The 1H2026 interim gives Rp14,376/kg [F19] against a 1H2026 benchmark of about USD 1,122/t (Q1 1,081, Q2 1,164) at roughly Rp17,300/USD, a ratio of about 0.74; the nine-month ratio is similar, because the World Bank re-based its palm-oil series in January 2026 and the domestic price NSSS realises has lagged the international print [S0, S2]. NSSS sells entirely into the domestic market at the Indonesian reference-price-linked level [S4], which carries a discount to the Rotterdam/Pink Sheet series. We set 0.760, the mid-point of the 1H2026 and nine-month evidence and below the FY2025 audited ratio, and hold it flat so the forecast carries no price-recovery assumption beyond the deck itself. The 1H2026 0.74 uses an FX of Rp17,300/USD (1H26 realised Rp14,376/kg / 17,300 = USD831/t against a 1H26 benchmark of USD1,122/t); on the FY2025 benchmark and FX of Rp16,448/USD the same 0.76 would price FY2025 at USD765/t versus the audited USD846.9/t. The calibration gate re-prices FY2025 volume at the FY2025 benchmark, so its -32% gap is decomposed line by line in qc_justifications (calibration.ebitda): realisation -Rp175bn at the gate FX, the filed 9M26 cost step -Rp329bn, FX +Rp116bn, the opex ratio +Rp47bn and other revenue -Rp10bn, summing to -Rp351bn.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no domestic price cap applies to Indonesian CPO sales; the B50 mandate is a demand driver, not a ceiling on NSSS's selling price [S4].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Palm oil cost intensity is expressed per tonne of CPO, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a plantation [S3].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (IDR)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last actual, the nine-month 2026 interim, escalated with IDR inflation. COGS of Rp1,001.587bn [S2] less depreciation charged to COGS of Rp117.958bn [S2] leaves Rp883.629bn of cash cost for the nine months; over about 99 kt of CPO sold that is Rp8.93m per tonne. The step up from the FY2025 audited Rp6.26m/t (Rp919.572bn COGS less Rp154.260bn depreciation [F7, F9] over 122.3 kt [F1]) is in the LK, not assumed: raw materials used rose to Rp157.958bn from Rp42.634bn a year earlier (external FFB purchases) and direct labour to Rp446.652bn from Rp293.419bn [S2]. We hold the nine-month unit cost rather than the lower FY2025 level, and escalate 2.5% a year with the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation [S0].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine scalar set to zero: the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS, so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S3].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling, port and the special-terminal logistics are already inside the per-tonne CPO cash cost backed out of the nine-month COGS [S2]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: 100% of revenue is domestic [S4] and the FY2025 cost-of-sales note carries no royalty or export-levy line; Indonesia's CPO export levy is borne by the exporter at shipment and does not apply to NSSS's domestic sales to SMAR, Karyaindah and Bina Karya Prima [S3, F30].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (palm kernel)
assumptions.basis: Palm kernel is the only other product. FY2025 PK sales were 26,699 t at Rp11,598/kg [F14, F15], or Rp309.7bn; FY2026E carries Rp300bn because the nine-month ASP is running near Rp13,000/kg on roughly 21 kt [S2], and then escalates 2.5% a year with IDR inflation [S0]. Kernel output tracks CPO throughput, so no separate volume build is needed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 100%: palm kernel is a by-product of FFB already harvested and processed for CPO, and its entire cash cost is carried in the per-tonne CPO cost above. Setting the kernel margin to 1.0 reconciles exactly to the audited FY2025 gross profit (CPO revenue Rp1,704.1bn less cash COGS Rp765.3bn plus PK revenue Rp309.7bn = Rp1,248.5bn before D&A) [F1, F7, F9, F14, F15].

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation charged to operations was Rp156.128bn (Rp154.260bn in COGS plus Rp1.868bn in G&A, [F9]) over 122.3 kt of CPO sold [F1], or Rp1.276m/t; the nine-month 2026 charge of Rp119.728bn over about 99 kt gives Rp1.21m/t [S2]. We carry Rp1.24m/t, between the two, and escalate 2.5% with IDR inflation. The Yahoo pack's Rp4.9bn D&A line is the direct-method cash-flow artefact and is replaced by the audited note figure.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (IDR)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capex only, matching the volume the existing estate delivers. FY2025 fixed-asset additions were Rp101.298bn [F13] plus plasma receivables of Rp69.453bn [S3] over 122.3 kt of CPO sold = Rp1.395m/t; the nine-month 2026 fixed-asset and plasma run-rate is about Rp1.245m/t [S2]. We carry Rp1.12m/t, which strips out the Rp34.119bn of nursery/land clearing in the FY2025 investing line [S3] (0.279m/t): the ~1,500 ha/yr new-planting programme is NOT credited with volume in this base (the volume path comes from maturing palms and OER), so its capex is removed rather than charged against an unvalued asset. The 16,501 ha unplanted landbank is valued separately in valuation.bridge at a transaction-comp basis, not through this line [F22].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: The third CPO mill at PMM carries an estimated capex of Rp270bn, scheduled in the 2027-28 capacity-expansion phase [F32]; we split it Rp135bn in each year. No other discrete project is disclosed, and the new plantings and land clearing are already in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9%: receivables plus inventories less payables were Rp203.2bn at 31-Dec-2025, 10.1% of revenue [F5, S3], and Rp202.7bn at 30-Sep-2026 on an annualised revenue base, about 11.6% [S2]. The balance is mostly inventory and the three domestic buyers settle in one to thirty days [S3], so 9% assumes part of the 2026 inventory build unwinds and is below the last actual, not above it.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22%: the nine-month 2026 effective rate is 22.4% (Rp145.060bn tax on Rp646.359bn pre-tax, [S2]) and the 22% headline now applies in full; the FY2025 16.2% rate benefited from the utilisation of tax losses that are exhausted [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.5%: FY2025 finance costs were Rp149.881bn on average bank debt of about Rp1.9tn and the nine-month 2026 charge is Rp108.508bn on about Rp1.6tn [S3, S2], an annualised 9.0%; 8.5% sits just below the latest actual because the group is amortising the BRI/BMRI facilities.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.3%: nine-month 2026 finance income of Rp30.053bn on average cash and deposits near Rp700bn [S2], down from 5.2% in FY2025 (Rp7.804bn on opening cash of Rp386bn plus the 2025 build).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The debt schedule restarts from the 30-Sep-2026 balance. Total interest-bearing debt was Rp1,575.3bn then: bank loans Rp1,560.7bn (short-term Rp115.962bn, current maturities Rp349.466bn and long-term Rp1,095.306bn) plus consumer-finance payables Rp11.403bn and lease liabilities Rp3.126bn [S2], against Rp1,765.5bn at 31-Dec-2025 [S3]. We therefore book the observed nine-month repayment of Rp190.2bn in FY2026E and zero thereafter; no new facility is disclosed and the third mill is assumed funded from cash flow [F32]. The FY2026E interest line is still struck on the 31-Dec-2025 opening balance at the 8.5% cost of debt, so it is not understated by the intra-year repayment.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: the nine-month 2026 Rp47.814bn of other operating income and the Rp11.400bn biological-asset fair-value gain are non-recurring marks and are excluded from the base [S2]; no recurring non-operating line is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: the subsidiaries are 99.99% owned and non-controlling interests are Rp10m against a Rp2,323bn equity base [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 20% of earnings: the group paid Rp71.4bn in FY2025 (11% of net profit) and Rp119.0bn (Rp5 per share) in the first nine months of 2026, 18% of FY2025 profit [S3, F31]; with net debt still Rp0.7tn and the third mill to fund, a 20% payout is the most likely path, not the maximum.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 23,801,568,645 shares in issue at 31-Dec-2025 and no dilutive instruments outstanding [F16, S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation [S0]: CPO prices and the IDR cost base escalate together, so real free cash flow is flat after the explicit years. It is not a volume-growth assumption, since the plantings and mill capacity cap output.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 5.0%: selling plus general and administrative expenses were Rp72.682bn in the nine months of 2026, 4.2% of revenue [S2], and Rp143.918bn in FY2025, 7.1% [S0]; the FY2025 figure includes the SK36 provision that is not recurring. 5.0% sits between the two and is held flat. It is deliberately NOT a clean number: the FY2025 audit note [S3 p5] says that if PP45 were applied in full, general and administrative expenses would rise by a further Rp368bn and other operating expenses by Rp78bn. That ~Rp446bn pre-tax hit is a bear-case item booked separately in the risk section, not annualised into the base (it relates to a one-off regulatory settlement, not the run-rate); the base opex therefore assumes the SK process settles near the booked Rp56.7bn provision rather than the PP45 maximum.

challenges.challenge: The 25%/15% cross-checks use 14.33x EV/EBITDA and 4.01x P/BV, labelled 'average of peer median and own five-year average' and explained in section 4 as 'the house plantation peer set currently trades at a median of 14.3 times trailing EBITDA'. The desk's own peer medians are 6.09x EV/EBITDA and 1.32x P/BV; 14.33x and 4.01x are exactly the average of those with NSSS's own n=3 means of 22.57x and 6.71x, and NSSS listed in March 2023 so no five-year history exists. The +82% divergence is self-anchoring on the stock's own post-IPO multiples (Rp366-2,180 in the last year), not a sector re-rating.
challenges.answer: Set valuation.multiple_source: peer_median so the cross-checks are 6.1x EV/EBITDA and 1.3x P/BV, and rewrote section 4 to label them as peer medians and explain the -30%/-68% divergences. Removed the own-history blend: NSSS listed Mar-2023, the n=3 means come from the same price spike. DCF 60% + peer EV 25% + peer P/BV 15% gives v0 Rp322, target Rp346, SELL.

challenges.challenge: calibration.ebitda is justified wholly on cost (Rp8.93m/t vs Rp6.26m/t [S2]), but the -32% (Rp351bn) gap also contains the realisation drift: the model re-prices FY+1 at USD765.3/t (0.76 x 1,007) against the audited USD846.9/t, worth ~Rp164bn, 47% of the gap, at the FY2025 FX of 16,448. The gate asks to reconcile costs, royalty OR realisation; only cost is addressed, so the largest BLOCK is half-answered and a price-driven gap is described as a cost-driven one.
challenges.answer: Rewrote qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda to split the -32% gap: ~Rp164bn realisation (0.841 to 0.76 at the FY2025 benchmark and FX Rp16,448) and ~Rp187bn from the filed 9M26 cash-cost step, and stated that 0.76 was calibrated at Rp17,300/USD. Both components reconciled, not cost alone.

challenges.challenge: The FFB yield of 9.7 t/ha is a first-half figure: S4 shows quarterly 5.2 and 4.5 t/ha and 1H25/1H26 at 9.7/9.7, and 257.2 kt of nucleus FFB over ~26.5k ha gives 9.7 for six months, so the annual nucleus yield is ~19.4 t/ha (401 kt harvested in 9M26 [F20]). The drift.volume justification's own arithmetic, 28,204 ha x 9.7 t/ha x 22.5% OER, gives 61.6 kt CPO, less than half the 130 kt it defends, and the section 7 monitor 'a yield below 9.7 t/ha' is already breached on an annual basis.
challenges.answer: Restated yield annually: FY2025 541.1 kt harvested over 28,204 ha is ~19.2 t/ha; 9.7 t/ha is a half-year figure. Rebuilt the volume basis on annual yield plus 80% utilisation, and reset the section 7 monitor to compare the half-year print against 9.7 t/ha.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025 audit note [S3 p5] quantifies the PP45 framework: had the SK36 provision been recognised as PP45 requires, accrued expenses, G&A and other operating expenses would each rise by Rp368bn, fixed assets fall Rp78bn, deferred tax liability Rp114bn and tax expense Rp114bn, against the Rp56.7bn provision and Rp51.7bn impairment booked [F28, F29]. That is ~Rp311bn of incremental pre-tax expense (~Rp263bn net, ~Rp11/share, 47% of FY2026E net profit). It appears nowhere in the report or the bear case, and it is why the 5.0% opex basis that strips the SK charge as non-recurring is optimistic.
challenges.answer: Added F36/F37/F38 (Rp368bn/Rp78bn/Rp114bn) from the FY2025 PP45 note and put the exposure in section 3 earnings quality, section 5 regulatory risk and the bear narrative; justified the opex basis as an explicit settlement assumption, not a view that PP45 is harmless.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 and the summary use the IDX review as a one-way governance cap but omit S6's own exculpatory detail: NSSS's 52% concentration is the lowest of the three names examined, over the longest window (1 Dec 2025 to 30 Oct 2026) with the most investors (19) and brokers (15), and BEI framed the letter as supervision, not a finding of wrongdoing. There is no sanction, no pledge disclosure in the audit and no rights issue in the record.
challenges.answer: Stated in sections 5 and 6 and the thesis that NSSS's 52% was the lowest of the three names, over the longest window with the most participants, and that BEI called it supervision not a finding; the discount is now attributed to the thin float and register, not the review.

challenges.challenge: The 16,501 ha unplanted landbank [F22] carries zero value anywhere (no holdings line, volume capped at 150 kt to 2035) yet capex_unit charges new planting and land clearing, ~1,500 ha planned in 2026 [S4], every year with no matching volume. Either the landbank is worth something (at USD2,000-4,000/ha unplanted that is Rp24-49/share) or the capex is wasted (PV ~Rp9/share). The bull case gives it nothing and the report calls it the long-run option without a number.
challenges.answer: Valued the 16,501 ha unplanted landbank as a Rp477bn bridge item at 25% of the POSCO/Sampoerna Agro transaction value per hectare, and removed the nursery/land-clearing capex from capex_unit so the asset is neither charged nor double-counted. The bridge applies in every scenario including bull.

challenges.challenge: The scenarios are not as symmetric as section 5 claims. The bull narrative says the third mill lifts OER to 23% and the domestic discount narrows as B50 absorbs supply, but the shocks are only CPO x1.2 and volume x1.05, with no OER and no realisation recovery, even though section 7 says a realisation recovering toward the audited FY2025 level would lift value toward the bull case. Restoring realisation to 0.841 in the bull takes it from Rp553 to ~Rp640 (+19% on today's price), adding ~Rp22 to the target at 25%.
challenges.answer: Bull now shocks realisation x1.107 (0.76 back to the audited 0.841) as well as CPO x1.2 and volume x1.06 for the OER/maturity uplift; bear mirrors with realisation x0.903. Bull value Rp512, still below the Rp540 price.

challenges.challenge: Sections 4 and 5 both say every hundred dollars a tonne on CPO is worth roughly a fifth of the equity value [S0]. The model's own grid moves value from 370.7 at 0.9x deck to 424.5 at 1.0x, +12.7% for USD124/t, i.e. ~10.2% per USD100/t; the stated sensitivity is overstated about two-fold, and section 5 uses it to rate the CPO risk as high impact. The grid is also labelled 12-month value with metric tp but reports v0 (424.5 at 1.0x/1.0x) against a stated TP of 472.5.

(2) Cash cost -Rp329bn: (Rp8.93m/t - Rp6.24m/t) x 122.333 kt = ~Rp329bn, where Rp8.93m/t is the filed 9M26 cash cost (COGS Rp1,001.6bn less depreciation Rp118.0bn over the CPO sold) against the audited FY2025 Rp6.24m/t, the step is visible in the 9M filing comparatives, with raw materials of Rp158.0bn in 9M2026 against Rp42.6bn in 9M2025 and direct labour of Rp446.7bn against Rp293.4bn [S2 p79], while the audited full-year accounts put FY2025 raw materials at Rp63.6bn and direct labour at Rp433.2bn [S3 p89], so the step is not a 9M-only artifact. This is the full filed step, not a residual. (3) FX +Rp116bn: the gate converts at 17,570/USD against the FY2025 average of 16,448/USD [S0], lifting revenue on the same dollar price. (4) Opex ratio +Rp47bn: the model opex ratio is below the audited FY2025 ratio because the pack treats the Decree No. 36 charges as non-recurring [S0, S3]. (5) Other revenue -Rp10bn: the gate re-prices only CPO volume and leaves out part of the kernel and other revenue [S0]. -175 -329 +116 +47 -10 = -Rp351bn. Each component is carried deliberately; none is a default haircut, and re-pricing at FY2025 cost alone would only redistribute the same gap.

flags.message: a.volume moves +15% from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The +15% from FY2026E to the long-run 150 kt is a maturity/OER path, not a price-led volume bet. Annual FFB yield is ~19.2 t/ha: FY2025 harvested 541.1 kt over 28,204 planted ha [F35, F21]; the 9.7 t/ha in the 1H26 deck [F23] is a half-year figure (quarterly 5.2 and 4.5 t/ha), so it must not be annualised twice. FY2026E-FY2027E are held at the guided ~80% utilisation of the existing 720,000 t FFB mills (576 kt FFB x 22.5% OER = 129.6 kt CPO) [S4, F25, F24], not grown. From 2028 the company's phase-02 third mill adds up to 60 t/hr "to support maturing estate yield curves", new mill technology lifts OER "up to 23% from current 22%" [S4, F32], and maturing palms lift annual yield toward ~22 t/ha, taking volume to 138 kt in FY2028E and 147 kt by FY2030E, capped at 150 kt - below the post-third-mill 1,080,000 t capacity at 80%. Purchased FFB stays near the 9M26 run-rate (~60 kt annualised), not the 132 kt a constant-harvest assumption would require [S2].
